_about: Text for the Natal and Far North roads (research.md sections 15-19): places, forks, events, warnings and the history pages after the ending. Deaths in the history are told plainly, never how.
place.kerkenberg.desc: Trekker wagons on the high grass at the very edge of the Drakensberg. Beyond the rim the land drops away into Natal, green and far below.
place.bloukrans.desc: Small trekker camps strung out along the Bloukrans and Bushman's rivers below the mountains: wagons, cattle, smoke, and green grass to the horizon.
place.port_natal.desc: A few houses of wattle and reed by a wide bay, a mission on the hill, and the sea. The traders here deal in ivory and hides.
place.magaliesberg.desc: A long ridge running east and west across the grassland. The hunters call it the Cashan Mountains. This is country the Ndebele claim.
place.strydpoort.desc: A gap through rocky hills, which the trekkers call Sekwati's poort after the Pedi chief whose people live in these hills.
place.soutpansberg.desc: A long blue mountain with a salt pan at its western end, and below it the country of the Venda. Tregardt's people built houses and a school here.
place.olifants_river.desc: A river running east toward the mountains and the low country. To follow it, you must cross it again and again.
place.escarpment.desc: The high country ends in cliffs and steep slopes. Far below, the low country lies blue in the haze. There is no road down.
place.lowveld.desc: Thorn trees, tall grass and heat. Game is everywhere, and so is the small brown fly that bites the oxen.
place.komati.desc: A broad river that runs through the Lebombo hills to the sea. The Portuguese fort is not far now.
place.delagoa_bay.desc: The Portuguese fort of Lourenco Marques: earth walls on a sand ridge by the bay, with a swamp behind.
history.place.kerkenberg: This is history: Retief camped at Kerkenberg with 54 wagons on 5 October 1837. The trekkers stayed there from mid-October to mid-November and sent men out to find ways down the escarpment. On 2 November Bantjes rode back up with word that they could come down into Natal. The trekkers used several passes. On the steep slopes the back wheels were taken off and heavy branches tied underneath, which dragged as a brake and kept the axles off the rocks.
history.place.bloukrans: This is history: in November 1837 the trekker families came down the Drakensberg and spread out in small camps along the Bloukrans and Bushman's rivers, near today's Estcourt and Weenen. Most of the people who trekked to Natal stopped here, waiting while Piet Retief went to the Zulu king Dingane to ask for land.
history.place.port_natal: This is history: Port Natal (later Durban) had about fifty English settlers and traders in 1835. Allen Gardiner had a mission on the hill above the bay, and American missionaries came in 1836. The traders welcomed Retief's riders on 19 October 1837.
history.place.magaliesberg: This is history: in 1837 the Ndebele under Mzilikazi held the country north of the Vaal. After the trekker attack on Mosega in January 1837 they were in the Marico, to the west, until a second commando in November 1837 drove them north over the Limpopo. The hunter Harris called this ridge the Cashan Mountains in 1836.
history.place.strydpoort: This is history: Tregardt's diary calls this gap 'the poort of Sekwati', after the Pedi chief Sekwati, who was rebuilding his people's strength in these years. Later, Sekwati warned Tregardt that his wagons could never cross the mountains to the east.
history.place.soutpansberg: This is history: Louis Tregardt's party lived at the foot of the Soutpansberg for more than a year (1836-37), waiting for Potgieter, who never came. They built houses, a smithy and a school for 21 children, dug a water furrow and planted gardens. The Venda chief Ramabulana gave Tregardt land, though the sources disagree on when. On 23 August 1837 Tregardt left for Delagoa Bay.
history.place.delagoa_bay: This is history: Tregardt's party reached the fort at Lourenco Marques at three in the afternoon on 13 April 1838, with seven wagons. They fired a salute and nobody answered. The Portuguese, unsure what so many armed men wanted, kept their guns in the fort, but treated them kindly.
history.place.olifants_river: This is history: Tregardt's party reached the Olifants River on 2 October 1837 and followed it east toward the mountains, crossing it thirteen times because the hills pressed so close.
history.place.escarpment: This is history: the Drakensberg escarpment drops from the high country to the lowveld. Tregardt's party spent from 8 November 1837 to 25 January 1838 getting their wagons down it.
history.place.lowveld: This is history: the lowveld, the hot low country between the Drakensberg and the sea, was deadly in the summer rains: malaria for people, and the tsetse fly for cattle, oxen and horses. Much of it is now the Kruger National Park.
history.place.komati: This is history: Tregardt's party reached the Komati in late March 1838. A Portuguese officer met them there, and their heavy goods went on down the river by boat.
shop.kerkenberg_laager: Trading in the camp at Kerkenberg
shop.kerkenberg.keeper: A trekker waiting to go down
barter.pedi_strydpoort.greeting: Through an interpreter: "You have come a long way. What do you have?"
barter.pedi_strydpoort.needs: "Beads and cloth, and iron for hoes. We have sheep and grain."
barter.venda_soutpansberg.greeting: Through an interpreter: "The other white people traded with us too. What have you brought?"
barter.venda_soutpansberg.needs: "Beads, cloth and iron. We have cattle, sheep and plenty of grain."
barter.tsonga_lowveld: Tsonga people in the low country
barter.tsonga_lowveld.greeting: Through an interpreter: "We can sell you grain and meat. What do you give?"
barter.tsonga_lowveld.needs: "Beads, cloth, iron. Cattle do not live long here."
cause.malaria: malaria, the fever of the low country
notice.fever: {who} is shivering one hour and burning the next: the fever of the low country has come.
notice.fly: The fly sickness is in the herd: {n} of the {item} have died. Cattle sicken and die in this country; it is the bite of the small brown fly.
journal.fly: {n} of the {item} died of the fly sickness.
lock.dry_season_now: It is the dry season now
route.highveld.label: On north to the Sand River and the Vaal ({miles} miles to the Sand River)
route.highveld.advice: Potgieter's people say: "North over the Vaal there is open grass, good water and room for everyone. Natal is a trap behind the mountains."
route.natal.label: East to the Drakensberg and down into Natal ({miles} miles to Kerkenberg)
route.natal.advice: Retief's people say: "Natal is green and well watered, with a harbour for trade. The council voted for it. But the wagons must go down the Drakensberg, and the Zulu king Dingane has not yet given leave."
route.mooi.label: On to the Mooi River ({miles} miles)
route.mooi.advice: Potgieter has seen the Mooi River country. It is close now: good grass and water, and other trekkers settling.
route.far_north.label: The Far North, to the Soutpansberg ({miles} miles to the Magaliesberg)
route.far_north.advice: A hunter who has been north: "It is a long road, but the high ground is healthy. Tregardt's people are at the Soutpansberg. There are no stores beyond the Vaal, so carry all the food, powder and lead you can, and beads to trade. And whatever you do, don't go down into the low country in the rains: the fever kills people and the fly kills cattle."
event.vet_river_council.body: The camps at the Vet River are full of argument. On 6 June a meeting of the men adopted nine articles for the trekkers' government and voted to go to Natal. Not everyone agrees.
event.vet_river_council.natal.done: "Natal is a garden. There is a harbour, so we can trade with the world without the English in between. We only need the Zulu king's leave, and Retief will get it."
event.vet_river_council.north.done: "Why take the wagons down a mountain into the Zulu king's country? North of the Vaal there is grass enough for all of us, now that the Matabele have been driven back."
event.vet_river_council.leave: Keep out of it and see to the wagon
event.vet_river_council.leave.done: The argument goes on around the fires late into the night.
event.kerkenberg_camp.body: Retief's camp at Kerkenberg stands on the very edge of the Drakensberg. Men ride out every day to look for ways down. Some slopes look possible; others end in cliffs.
event.kerkenberg_camp.wait: Wait until the scouts find the best way down
event.kerkenberg_camp.wait.done: After a week of waiting a scout comes back with news of a slope that wagons can manage. It is steep, but there is a way.
event.kerkenberg_camp.together: Go down together with a trekker party
event.kerkenberg_camp.together.done: With many hands on the ropes and many oxen, the wagons go down one at a time. It takes days, but nobody is hurt.
event.kerkenberg_camp.now: Go down now by the first way found
event.kerkenberg_camp.now.ok: The back wheels are taken off and heavy branches tied underneath to drag as a brake. With everyone hauling back on the riems, the wagon slides and lurches down the slope and reaches the bottom in one piece.
event.kerkenberg_camp.now.bad: Halfway down, the branches tear loose and the wagon runs away from the riems and slams into a rock. The axle is cracked, and someone is hurt trying to hold it.
event.bloukrans_camps.body: Below the mountains, trekker families have spread out in small camps along the Bloukrans and Bushman's rivers. The grass is deep and the water is good. Everyone is waiting for news of Retief's talks with the Zulu king.
event.bloukrans_camps.stay: Make your home here with the other families
event.bloukrans_camps.stay.done: You choose a place by the river, unyoke the oxen and start to cut poles for a shelter. This is where your trek ends.
event.bloukrans_camps.go: Go on to Port Natal and the sea
event.bloukrans_camps.go.done: You rest a day, then turn the wagon toward the coast.
event.port_natal_arrival.body: At last: the bay, the sea, and a few houses of wattle and reed. English traders come down to look at the wagon, and a missionary rides over from the hill.
event.port_natal_arrival.outspan.done: The oxen are turned loose to graze, and for the first time in months you hear the sea.
event.magaliesberg_ndebele.body: Along the ridge you see cattle tracks and the marks of old villages. This is country the Ndebele claim. Their king, Mzilikazi, is at war with the trekkers, and his men may be watching.
event.magaliesberg_ndebele.gift: Send a gift of beads ahead with a message of peace
event.magaliesberg_ndebele.gift.done: Your messenger comes back safe. Nobody stops the wagon, and twice you see men on the ridge who watch you go by.
event.magaliesberg_ndebele.watch: Keep moving and keep a strong watch
event.magaliesberg_ndebele.watch.done: Nobody sleeps well, and the oxen are driven hard, but nothing happens.
event.strydpoort_sekwati.body: The road goes through a rocky gap in the hills. Pedi herders watch from the slopes. These are Sekwati's people, and this is his country.
event.strydpoort_sekwati.gift: Send a gift of beads to Sekwati
event.strydpoort_sekwati.gift.done: The gift is taken up the hill. Later some of Sekwati's people come down to trade.
event.strydpoort_sekwati.ask.done: "The Venda live under the long mountain to the north. White people with wagons are camped there. They have been there a year."
event.strydpoort_sekwati.go.done: The wagon creaks through the gap and out onto the plain beyond.
event.soutpansberg_camp.body: The long mountain rises out of the plain, blue and green. At its foot are fields, Venda villages and smoke, and the tracks of wagons.
event.soutpansberg_camp.visit.done: Louis Tregardt greets you himself. They have waited a year for Potgieter, who never came. Two Portuguese soldiers have come up from Delagoa Bay to guide them to the coast. "We have too many cattle to stay," he says. "We go round by the south, away from the fly."
event.soutpansberg_camp.empty: Look over the camp the trekkers left
event.soutpansberg_camp.empty.done: There are houses of poles and clay, a smithy, and a little schoolhouse with its door open. A Venda man tells you the white people left for the coast near the end of August, with Portuguese soldiers to show them the way.
event.soutpansberg_camp.goal: Tsonga traders who come up from the coast say the low country can only be crossed in winter. In the rains, they say, the fever is there, and the fly kills every ox. What will you do?
event.soutpansberg_camp.stay.done: You choose a place by the stream, near the old camp, and begin to build. Your trek ends here.
event.soutpansberg_camp.wait: Stay here until the winter, then go on to the coast
event.soutpansberg_camp.wait.done: You build a shelter, plant a garden and trade with the Venda for grain and sheep, as Tregardt's people did. The rains come and go. In April, when the grass turns brown, you yoke the oxen again.
event.soutpansberg_camp.go: Go on to Delagoa Bay now
event.soutpansberg_camp.go.done: You load the wagon and turn its nose toward the sea.
event.talk_soutpansberg.body: Under the Soutpansberg you can talk with the Venda, with the Tsonga traders who come up from the coast, and with anyone who knew Tregardt's people.
event.talk_soutpansberg.traders: Ask the Tsonga traders about the road to the coast
event.talk_soutpansberg.traders.done: "We come up in the winter, when the grass is dry. In the summer rains nobody crosses the low country: the fever is in the air there, and the fly kills cattle. Go in the winter, or don't go."
event.talk_soutpansberg.pretorius: Ask what happened to the people who went east last year
event.talk_soutpansberg.pretorius.done: "Some of Tregardt's people went east into the low country to look for the Van Rensburgs. Tregardt warned them not to go. The fever caught them and the fly killed their oxen until they could not move. Gert Scheepers died on the way back."
event.talk_soutpansberg.rensburg: Ask about the Van Rensburg party
event.talk_soutpansberg.rensburg.done: "They went ahead toward the coast in the winter of last year, forty-nine people. They were all killed near the great river. Nobody here knows the whole of it."
event.olifants_warning.body: A messenger comes from Sekwati: the mountains to the east cannot be crossed with wagons. "Go back," he says. "There is no way through for you."
event.olifants_warning.thank: Thank him and send tobacco back to Sekwati
event.olifants_warning.thank.done: The messenger takes the tobacco and goes. You look east at the mountains and wonder if he is right.
event.olifants_warning.go: Go on down the river anyway
event.olifants_warning.go.done: Tregardt didn't believe the warning either. The wagon goes on down the river, crossing it again and again.
event.escarpment_descent.body: The road ends at the edge of the Drakensberg. Below, far below, lies the low country. There is no wagon road down: only steep slopes, rocks and cliffs, and mist every afternoon.
event.escarpment_descent.road: Make a road down: cut, dig and level, however long it takes
event.escarpment_descent.road.done: Week after week you cut through bush, roll rocks aside and dig a shelf for the wheels where the slope is too steep. On the worst slopes the back wheels are taken off and tied to a sledge. After nearly six weeks the wagon stands at the bottom. Everyone is worn out, and two oxen fell and did not get up.
event.escarpment_descent.road.long: Rain and mist stop the work again and again. Some days you make no more than a few yards. Two months go by before the wagon is down. People are thin and tired, and several animals have been lost on the slopes.
event.escarpment_descent.apart: Take the wagon apart and carry it down piece by piece
event.escarpment_descent.apart.done: Wheels, axles, bed and tent come off, and everything is carried and lowered down the slope on backs and ropes. It is faster than making a road, but parts are scraped and cracked, and the tent is torn. After nearly four weeks you put it all together again at the bottom.
event.escarpment_descent.scout: Spend a week looking for a better way
event.escarpment_descent.scout.done: The men ride along the edge for a week. Every way down is as bad as the last.
event.lowveld_fly.body: The low country is hot and thick with thorn bush. Small brown flies settle on the oxen, and the cattle are listless. The people who live here keep few cattle, or none.
event.lowveld_fly.guide: Give beads to a local man to guide you by the quickest way
event.lowveld_fly.guide.done: He leads you along paths between the thickets, to water every evening. You make better time than you hoped.
event.lowveld_fly.push: Push on as fast as the oxen can go
event.lowveld_fly.push.done: You drive the oxen hard through the heat. The sooner you are out of this country, the better.
event.lowveld_fly.rest: Rest the oxen for two days first
event.lowveld_fly.rest.done: The oxen rest, but the flies do not.
event.komati_portuguese.body: At the Komati a Portuguese officer rides out from the fort with a few soldiers to meet you. He offers boats to take your heavy goods down the river.
event.komati_portuguese.boat: Send the heavy goods down the river by boat
event.komati_portuguese.boat.done: With the wagon lighter, the weak oxen can manage the last miles.
event.komati_portuguese.together: Keep everything on the wagon and go on with him
event.komati_portuguese.together.done: The officer rides beside you and points out the way.
event.delagoa_arrival.body: Lourenco Marques at last: a small earth fort on a sand ridge by the bay, with a swamp behind it. You fire a salute with the guns. Nobody answers. Then the commandant comes out, greets you kindly, and asks for your guns, to be kept in the fort while you are here.
event.delagoa_arrival.guns.done: The guns are carried into the fort. The Portuguese find houses for you in the town.
event.delagoa_arrival.argue.done: There is no help for it. The guns go into the fort.
event.tsonga_traders_road.body: A line of Tsonga traders passes, carrying goods from the coast on their heads and shoulders: cloth, beads and brass wire.
event.tsonga_traders_road.trade.done: The trade is done with much laughing and pointing.
event.tsonga_traders_road.ask: Ask them about the road to the coast
event.tsonga_traders_road.ask.done: "We cross the low country in winter. In summer, nobody goes: fever."
event.far_north_lead.body: The lead is running short, and there is nowhere to buy more this far north.
event.far_north_lead.melt: Melt down iron scraps and odds and ends for bullets
event.far_north_lead.melt.done: The bullets are rough, but they will shoot.
event.far_north_lead.save: Save what is left for emergencies
event.far_north_lead.save.done: No more shooting for the pot unless there is no other way.
event.fever_low_country.body: The air is heavy and the evenings are loud with insects. Everyone knows the low country brings fever. People say it rises from the swamps and the wet ground at night.
event.fever_low_country.high: Camp on higher ground, away from the water
event.fever_low_country.high.done: You make camp on a rise. It is a long walk to water, but it feels safer.
event.fever_low_country.on.done: You camp by the water. The insects whine around the fire all night.
event.natal_green.body: Natal is as green as they said. The grass comes up to the oxen's bellies, streams run in every valley, and the air is soft.
event.natal_green.rest: Rest a day and let the oxen graze
event.natal_green.rest.done: The oxen eat until they can eat no more. The children run in the long grass.
event.natal_green.on.done: Even the oxen seem to walk more easily.
event.natal_messengers.body: Zulu messengers pass the wagon at a run, heading for the king's place. They look at the wagon, and go on without stopping.
event.natal_messengers.greet.done: One of them raises a hand without breaking his stride.
event.natal_messengers.watch: Watch them go and wonder what news they carry
event.natal_messengers.watch.done: That night the talk at the fire is all of Retief and the king.
history.vet_river_council: This is history: on 6 June 1837 a meeting of 140 men at the Little Vet River adopted nine articles for the trekkers' government and chose Port Natal and Natal as their goal. Potgieter was against going to Natal and stayed on the Highveld.
history.olifants_warning: This is history: the Pedi chief Sekwati warned Tregardt that the mountains to the east were impassable for wagons. Tregardt did not trust the warning and went on down the Olifants River, crossing it again and again. Sekwati was very nearly right.
history.escarpment_descent: This is history: Tregardt's party made a road down the escarpment from 8 November 1837 to 25 January 1838, two months and eighteen days, in heavy rain and mist. The men nearly gave up and talked of leaving the wagons; the women would not hear of it. On steep slopes they took off the back wheels and tied them on a sledge, and tied the rear oxen to the front axle so they would not fall. Jan Pretorius took his wagons apart and carried them down piece by piece.
history.lowveld_fly: This is history: in February and March 1838, 'the unhealthiest months of the year', Tregardt's cattle died of the 'bush sickness'. It was nagana, carried by the tsetse fly, which kills cattle, oxen and horses but not people. 'Fly disease' was first recorded in this country in 1836. Of about 480 cattle in March, most were dead within weeks.
history.komati_portuguese: This is history: at the Komati a Portuguese officer from the fort met Tregardt's party. Their ivory and heavy goods went down the river by boat while the wagons struggled on behind their weak oxen.
history.tsonga_traders: This is history: Tsonga traders, whom Tregardt calls Magwambas, came up from Delagoa Bay to the Soutpansberg every winter. They crossed the low country in the dry season, when the fever and the fly were least.
history.far_north_lead: This is history: by 1837-38 Tregardt's party had about one keg of powder left and melted tin and copper to make bullets.
history.fever: This is history: people called malaria 'the fever' and blamed the swamps, the night air and the rains. In fact it is carried by mosquitoes, which breed in the warm, wet low country in summer; nobody knew that until 1897. Camping on high ground helped only a little. Quinine was known in Europe, but there is no sign the trekkers had it, and a missionary wrote that nobody at Delagoa Bay knew any medicine.
history.natal_green: This is history: in 1834 Piet Uys led 21 people to scout Natal. They came back with good reports of green, well-watered land, and those reports helped start the Great Trek.
history.natal_messengers: This is history: from November 1837 Retief negotiated with the Zulu king Dingane for land in Natal, while the trekker families waited in the camps below the mountains. The messengers here are invented.
map.other_sheet: Tab or the arrow keys: the other map.
ending.history.title: What happened next
ending.footer.more: Enter: what happened next.  M: the map of your road.

epilogue.mooi.1: Your family stopped where Potgieter's people settled. In November 1837 a trekker commando drove the Ndebele north over the Limpopo, and the trekkers took the country between the Vaal and the Limpopo for themselves.
epilogue.mooi.2: Potchefstroom was founded on the Mooi River in 1838 or 1839 (the sources disagree). It became the first capital of the trekker republic north of the Vaal.
epilogue.mooi.3: The Barolong, Bahurutshe and others who had lived in this country before the wars came back to find it claimed by the newcomers. Their story is part of this one.
epilogue.natal.1: On 6 February 1838 Piet Retief and about a hundred of his party, trekkers and servants, were killed at the Zulu king Dingane's capital, after the king had signed a paper giving them land.
epilogue.natal.2: On the night of 17 February 1838 Zulu regiments attacked the trekker camps along the Bloukrans and Bushman's rivers. About 282 trekkers were killed, 185 of them children, and about 250 Khoikhoi and Basotho who travelled with them. Some camps held out. The town later built there is called Weenen: 'weeping'.
epilogue.natal.3: Many families in these camps did not survive that night. Your family's story ends before it, but theirs did not.
epilogue.natal.4: In April 1838 Piet Uys and his young son Dirkie were killed at Italeni. On 16 December 1838 a trekker commando defeated Dingane's army at Blood River. The trekkers' Republic of Natalia lasted until Britain took Natal in 1843, and most of the trekkers then left again for the Highveld.
epilogue.natal.5: Dingane had reasons of his own: he had seen the trekkers drive the Ndebele out of their country, and he feared for his. How these events are remembered has been argued over ever since.
epilogue.port_natal.1: Port Natal's traders had welcomed the trekkers. In April 1838 they raised a force of their own against Dingane under Robert Biggar. It was defeated at the Tugela on 17 April, and few came back.
epilogue.port_natal.2: The Zulu army then came to the bay. Most of the people at Port Natal escaped on a ship that happened to be in the harbour, the Comet, and watched the settlement plundered from the water. Blown north to Delagoa Bay, the Comet found Tregardt's people dying of fever there.
epilogue.port_natal.4: Port Natal became Durban. In 1842 British troops besieged the trekkers there, and Dick King rode 600 miles to Grahamstown for help. In 1843 Natal became a British colony.
epilogue.soutpansberg.1: Your family stopped where Tregardt's people had lived for a year. Tregardt himself went on to the coast.
epilogue.soutpansberg.2: Tregardt's party reached Delagoa Bay on 13 April 1838, in the fever season. His wife Martha died on 1 May 1838, and he died on 25 October 1838. About half the party died at the bay, most of them of malaria.
epilogue.soutpansberg.3: The trekkers came back to the Soutpansberg in 1848, when part of Potgieter's trek founded a village there, later called Schoemansdal. It was abandoned in 1867. The Venda remained.
epilogue.far_north.1: Only 26 of Tregardt's party, most of them children, were still alive when a ship took them to Port Natal in July 1839. The Van Rensburg party, 49 people who had gone ahead toward the coast in 1836, had all been killed.
epilogue.delagoa.1: Your family reached the bay as Tregardt's did. What happened to his people shows what the fever season meant.
epilogue.delagoa.2: Four days after they arrived, Tregardt's wife, three children and the old teacher Daniel Pfeffer fell ill. Pfeffer died on 21 April 1838. Martha Tregardt died on 1 May 1838, and Tregardt stopped writing his diary.
epilogue.delagoa.3: The Rev. Francis Owen, passing in May, wrote that nearly everyone was ill and that nobody at the bay knew any medicine, though the Portuguese were very kind. Louis Tregardt died on 25 October 1838.
epilogue.delagoa.4: News reached the trekkers in Natal in February 1839. The ship Mazeppa sailed to fetch the survivors and landed them at Port Natal on 19 July 1839.
